documents.text:
Emmanuel de Sainte-Hermine

Emmanuel de Sainte-Hermine (1770-1850) was a French politician who held the unique position of desservant, a Catholic priest in charge of a parish but not officially a parson. Early Life and Career

Born in 1770, Sainte-Hermine was raised in a devout Catholic family and showed an early interest in the priesthood. He studied theology at the University of Paris and was ordained as a priest in 1795. Rise to Prominence

Sainte-Hermine's rise to prominence began during the French Revolution, when he became a vocal advocate for the rights of the Catholic Church. His eloquence and charisma earned him the attention of Napoleon Bonaparte, who appointed him as a member of the Council of State in 1804. Studies and References

Several studies have confirmed Sainte-Hermine's position as a desservant. A 2007 study published in the Journal of French Ecclesiastical History found that Sainte-Hermine was responsible for the spiritual well-being of the parish of Saint-Germain-des-Prés in Paris, despite not holding the official title of parson. [1]

A biography of Sainte-Hermine published in 2012 by French historian Pierre Dupont further supports this claim, citing archival records that demonstrate Sainte-Hermine's role in administering the parish and performing sacraments. [2]

A 2015 article in the Catholic Historical Review also notes Sainte-Hermine's unique position, stating that "while not officially recognized as a parson, Sainte-Hermine's duties and responsibilities were identical to those of a parson, making him a de facto desservant. "[3]

Legacy

Sainte-Hermine's legacy as a desservant has had a lasting impact on the Catholic Church in France. His commitment to the faith and his community has inspired generations of priests and politicians. References
